title: 論語 堯曰第二十
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 20, 〈堯曰〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 20 of the Analects, 堯曰 Yáo yuē, named, as every book is, from its first words — "Yao said". The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Book 20 is the last and the shortest, three passages in all. The first is not a saying of the Master's at all but a string of words and deeds of the founding kings: Yao's charge to Shun as he hands on the throne (the order Heaven reckons out now rests in you; hold truly to the mean), given again by Shun to Yu; Tang's declaration to the High Lord on Heaven as he overthrows the Xia (the guilt of the people lies on me); and King Wu's gifts to good men, his words on humane men and kin, and his work of government — true weights and measures, lapsed offices filled, fallen states and broken lines restored (20.1). Zhu Xi quotes Yang Shi: the book ends with these to show that what the sages' learning hands down is one and the same. In the second, Zizhang asks what fits a man to govern, and the Master names five excellences and four evils, which Zhu Xi, quoting Yin Tun, calls the most complete answer on government anywhere in the Analects (20.2). The third is the last saying of the Analects: without knowing the decree, the rites and words, one cannot be a gentleman, stand, or know men (20.3). Each numbered passage begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
堯曰：「
咨！爾舜！
天之厯數在爾躬，允執其中。
四海困窮，天禄永終。」

morph.gloss: at the end of their means

sentences.l:
Yao said:
“Ah! You, Shun!
Heaven's reckoned order rests in your person; truly hold to its mean.
If those within the four seas are hard pressed and at the end of their means, Heaven's emolument ends for ever.”
sentences.i: Yao said: “Ah, Shun! The line that Heaven counts out from reign to reign has come round to you. Keep faithfully to the mean. Let the people within the four seas be driven to want, and what Heaven allotted you is gone for good.”
sentences.n: The last book is named 堯曰 from its opening words. Zhu Xi counts three chapters (凡三章); our numbers are his. 堯 Yao is the sage king of high antiquity (8.19), 舜 Shun the man he raised to succeed him (12.22). Zhu Xi: these are the words with which Yao charged Shun and yielded him the throne (此堯命舜而禪以帝位之辭). 咨 zī is a sound of sighing (咨嗟歎聲), 'ah!'; 爾 'you'. 厯 is the edition's form of 曆 'reckoning', and 厯數 lì shù is, in Zhu Xi's words, the order in which emperors and kings follow one another, like the order of the seasons and the solar terms (帝王相繼之次第猶嵗時節氣之先後也); He Yan's unsigned comment: 'the order of succession' (暦數謂列次也). 躬 'one's own person'. 允 yǔn 'truly' (Zhu Xi and Bao Xian: 允信也). 中 zhōng 'the mean' — Zhu Xi: the name for neither going too far nor falling short (無過不及之名). 困窮 'hard pressed, at the end of their means'; 禄 is the edition's form of 祿 'emolument', the portion a ruler holds from Heaven; 永 yǒng 'for ever'. Zhu Xi takes the last line as a warning: if the people within the four seas are in straits, the ruler's emolument too will be cut off for ever (四海之人困窮則君禄亦永絶矣戒之也). Bao Xian in He Yan reads it the other way, as a promise: 困 is 'utmost', 永 'long' — govern holding truly to the mean, and you can reach to the utmost of the four seas, and Heaven's emolument will last to the end (言爲政信執其中則能窮極四海天禄所以長終也).

sentences.l: Shun too charged Yu with them.
sentences.i: Shun in his turn gave the same charge to Yu.
sentences.n: 禹 Yu, the Great Yu, who tamed the flood and succeeded Shun (8.18). 以 'with (them)', the words just spoken; 命 'to charge, to command'. Zhu Xi: when Shun later yielded the throne to Yu, he too charged him with these words; they are now found in the Counsels of the Great Yu 大禹謨 in the Documents of Yu 虞書, at greater length (舜後遜位於禹亦以此辭命之今見於虞書大禹謨比此加詳). Kong Anguo in He Yan: Shun too charged Yu with the words of Yao's charge to himself (舜亦以堯命巳之辭命禹也).

sentences.t:
曰：「
予小子履敢用𤣥牡，敢昭告于皇皇后帝：
有罪不敢赦。帝臣不蔽，簡在帝心。
朕躬有罪，無以萬方；萬方有罪，罪在朕躬。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
(Tang) said:
“I, the little child Lü, presume to use a black bull, and presume openly to announce to the most august Sovereign, the High Lord:
the guilty I dare not pardon; the High Lord's servants I do not hide; the sorting lies in the High Lord's heart.
If my person has guilt, lay it not on the ten thousand regions; if the ten thousand regions have guilt, the guilt lies on my person.”
sentences.i: And Tang said: “I, Lü, a small child before you, make bold to offer a black bull and to declare plainly to the great and glorious Lord on High: the guilty man I dare not let go, and those who serve you I will not keep hidden; it is for your heart to pick them out. If I myself do wrong, let it not be set down against the peoples of the world; if the peoples of the world do wrong, let it be set down against me.”
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: these are the words of the Announcement of Tang 湯誥 in the Documents of Shang, spoken after Tang had banished Jie 桀, last king of the Xia, and announced to the lords; they differ a little from the Documents' text (與書文大同小異). Before 曰 there should be the name 湯 (曰上當有湯字): Tang, founder of the Shang (12.22), whose personal name was 履 Lü (履盖湯名; Kong Anguo: 履殷湯名). 予 yú 'I'; 小子 'little child', a king's humble name for himself before Heaven. 敢 'to dare, to presume', the speaker's deference. 𤣥 is the edition's form of 玄 'black'; 牡 mǔ 'a male beast', the bull of sacrifice — Zhu Xi: the Xia esteemed black, and Tang had not yet changed its rites (夏尚黒未變其禮也); Kong Anguo in He Yan agrees: the Yin esteemed white but had not yet changed the Xia rites, so used a black bull (殷家尚白未變夏禮故用玄牡也). 昭 'openly, clearly'; 于 'to'. 皇皇 'most august'; 后 'sovereign'; 帝 dì 'the High Lord', the god of Heaven — Kong Anguo: 皇 is great, 后 is lord; 'great, great lord Di' means the Di of Heaven (皇大也右君也大大君帝謂天帝也, the print's 右 standing for 后). Zhu Xi explains the next lines: Jie had guilt, and Tang did not dare pardon him; the worthy men of the world are all the High Lord's servants, and Tang would not hide them; 簡 'to sort, to review' (簡閲也) — the choice lies in the High Lord's heart, to go as he commands (惟帝所命). These, he says, are the words with which Tang first sought the High Lord's command and attacked Jie. He Yan's unsigned comment takes 帝臣不蔽 of Jie: he sat in the place of the High Lord's servant, and his guilt could not be hidden (言桀居帝臣之位也有罪過不可隱蔽). 朕 zhèn 'I, my' (a pronoun of the speaker, used later only by emperors). 萬方 'the ten thousand regions', all the peoples. 無以萬方 'do not (lay it) on the ten thousand regions' — Kong Anguo: the ten thousand regions have no part in it (万方不與也). Zhu Xi: when the ruler has guilt it is not the people's doing, and when the people have guilt it is truly the ruler's doing — he is hard on himself and light on others (見其厚於責己薄於責人之意); these are the words of his announcement to the lords. Variant: He Yan's text reads 萬方有罪在朕躬 with one 罪, 'if the ten thousand regions have guilt, it lies on my person'.

sentences.t:
周有大賚，
善人是富。
sentences.l:
Zhou made a great bestowal:
it was good men that it enriched.
sentences.i: The Zhou gave out gifts on a great scale, and it was the good whom they made rich.
sentences.n: 周 Zhou, the dynasty that followed the Shang. 賚 lài 'to bestow, to give' (Zhu Xi: 賚來代反…賚予也). 善人是富 sets the object first and points back to it with 是: 'good men — these it enriched'. Zhu Xi: from here on the text tells of King Wu (此以下述武王事); when he had conquered the Shang he made a great bestowal across the four seas, as the Completion of the War 武成 in the Documents of Zhou records, and the passage says that those he made rich were all good men; the preface to the Ode 賚 in the Odes, 'the bestowal is how the good are given gifts' (賚所以錫予善人), probably rests on this. He Yan's unsigned comment reads it of Heaven's gift: the house of Zhou received a great bestowal from Heaven and was rich in good men — the 'ten ministers who bring order' (有亂臣十人是也; 8.20).

sentences.t:
雖有周親，不如仁人
百姓有過，在予一人。

morph.gloss: surname, clan name (同姓 'the same surname', Zhu Xi: 禮不娶同姓, 'the rites do not take a wife of one's own surname')

sentences.l:
Though there be the closest kin, they are not as good as humane men.
If the hundred clans have faults, they lie on me, the One Man.
sentences.i: Kinsmen, however near, are no match for men who are humane. If the people go astray, the blame is mine alone.
sentences.n: King Wu's own words, though the text gives him no 曰: Zhu Xi says they come from the Great Declaration 泰誓 in the Documents of Zhou, and quotes Mr Kong (孔氏, the Kong Anguo commentary on the Documents) there: 周 is 'utmost' (周至也) — Zhou 紂 of the Shang had many of his very closest kin, but not so many humane men as the house of Zhou (言紂至親雖多不如周家之多仁人). 仁人 'humane men'. 百姓 'the hundred clans', the whole people (12.9); 過 'fault, wrongdoing'. 予一人 'I, the One Man', a king's name for himself. He Yan's Kong Anguo reads the first line otherwise: kin who are not worthy and not loyal are put to death, as Guan and Cai were; humane men such as Jizi and Weizi came and were employed (親而不賢不忠則誅管蔡是也仁人箕子微子來則用也).

sentences.t:
謹權量，審法度，
脩廢官，四方之政行焉。
sentences.l:
Careful over weights and measures, scrutinising laws and standards,
restoring lapsed offices — the government of the four quarters went forward.
sentences.i: He took care that weights and measures were true, looked closely into laws and standards and filled again the offices that had fallen vacant, and government was carried through in every quarter.
sentences.n: The acts are still King Wu's, on Zhu Xi's reading, though no subject is named. 謹 'careful, attentive'. 權 quán 'the weight of a steelyard' (Zhu Xi: 權稱錘也); 量 liàng 'measures of capacity', the dou and the hu (量斗斛也; Bao Xian in He Yan the same). 審 shěn 'to examine closely'. 法 'law, model'; 度 dù 'standard, regulation' — Zhu Xi: rites and music and institutions are all meant by 法度 (法度禮樂制度皆是也). 脩 is the edition's form of 修 'to put in order, to restore'; 廢官 'offices left vacant'. 四方 'the four quarters'; 行 xíng 'to go forward, to take effect'; 焉 yān a final particle.

sentences.t:
興滅國，繼絶世，舉逸民，
天下之民歸心焉。

morph.gloss: left out, passed over (in 逸民, 夷逸, 18.8)

sentences.l:
Raising up extinguished states, continuing broken lines, promoting men left out of office —
the people of all under Heaven turned their hearts to him.
sentences.i: He brought back states that had been wiped out, restored lines that had died out and brought into office men who had been passed over, and all the people under Heaven gave him their hearts.
sentences.n: 興 xīng 'to raise up, to revive'; 滅 'to extinguish'. 繼 'to continue, to succeed to' (as 2.23 繼周 'succeed the Zhou'); 絶 is the edition's form of 絕 'broken off'; 世 'a line, a generation'. 舉 'to raise, to promote'; 逸民 'men left out of office' (18.8). 歸心 'to turn the heart to', with 焉 yān 'to him'. Zhu Xi: raising extinguished states and continuing broken lines means enfeoffing the descendants of the Yellow Emperor, Yao, Shun, the Xia and the Shang (封黄帝堯舜夏商之後); promoting men left out means freeing Jizi 箕子 from prison and restoring Shang Rong 商容 to his post (釋箕子之囚復商容之位); all three are what men's hearts desire (三者皆人心之所欲也).

sentences.l:
What he gave weight to:
the people, food, mourning, sacrifice.
sentences.i: Four things he held of great weight: the people, their food, mourning and sacrifice.
sentences.n: 所重 'what he gave weight to', 所 making a noun of the verb; 重 zhòng 'heavy, to treat as weighty'. 食 shí 'food'; 喪 sāng 'mourning'; 祭 jì 'sacrifice'. Zhu Xi cites only the Completion of the War 武成: 'he gave weight to the people's five teachings, and to food, mourning and sacrifice' (重民五教惟食喪祭). Kong Anguo in He Yan: he gave weight to the people, for they are the root of the state; to food, for it is the people's life; to mourning, as the way grief is fully spent; to sacrifice, as the way reverence is brought to the spirits (重民國之本也重食民之命也重䘮所以盡哀也重祭所以致敬也).

sentences.t:
寛則得衆，信則民任焉，
敏則有功，公則説。
sentences.l:
Broad-minded, and you win the many; true to your word, and the people rely on you;
quick, and you achieve things; fair, and they are pleased.
sentences.i: Be broad-minded, and the many come over to you; keep your word, and the people put their weight on you; be quick, and things get done; be fair, and they are glad.
sentences.n: The first three clauses are those of 17.6, with 民 'the people' for 人, and our English is kept from there. 寛 is the edition's form of 寬 'broad-minded'; 衆 'the many'. 任 rèn 'to rely on' (Zhu Xi at 17.6: 任倚仗也), with 焉 yān 'on him', here 'on you'. 敏 'quick'; 功 'achievement, results'. 公 'fair, impartial'; 説 is read yuè 'pleased' (説音悦). Zhu Xi: nothing of this is found among King Wu's acts; it is perhaps a general statement of the Way of emperors and kings (此於武王之事無所見恐或泛言帝王之道也). He then quotes Yang Shi on the whole chapter: the Analects records the sage's subtle words, which his followers handed down and kept to make this Way plain; so at the end of the book it sets out Yao's and Shun's words of charge, the purpose of Tang's and Wu's oaths to their armies, and what they did in government, to show that what the sage's learning hands down is one and the same (以明聖學之所傳者一於是而已) — the great point of all twenty books; and Mencius, in his last chapter, likewise sets out Yao, Shun, Tang, King Wen and Kongzi in succession. Variants: He Yan's text has no 信則民任焉 and reads 公則民說, 'fair, and the people are pleased'; Kong Anguo there: when government and teaching are fair the people are pleased, and all this is how the two emperors and three kings governed, so it was handed down to later ages.

sentences.t:
子張問於孔子曰：「何如斯可以從政矣？」
子曰：「尊五美，屏四惡，斯可以從政矣。」
子張曰：「何謂五美？」
子曰：「君子惠而不費，勞而不怨，欲而不貪，泰而不驕，威而不猛。」

sentences.l:
Zizhang asked Kongzi: “Being how, can one then take part in government?”
The Master said: “Honour the five excellences, put away the four evils — then you can take part in government.”
Zizhang said: “What is meant by the five excellences?”
The Master said: “The gentleman is kind and not wasteful, sets people to toil and is not resented, desires and is not greedy, is assured and not haughty, is imposing and yet not fierce.”
sentences.i: Zizhang asked Kongzi: “What must a man be like before he is fit to govern?” The Master said: “Let him hold to the five excellences and keep clear of the four evils, and he is fit to govern.” “What are the five excellences?” asked Zizhang. The Master said: “A gentleman is generous without being lavish; he works the people without their bearing him a grudge; he has desires but no greed; he has quiet assurance but no pride; he commands awe but not fear.”
sentences.n: 子張 Zizhang is the disciple Zhuansun Shi 顓孫師 (2.18). 問於孔子 'asked of Kongzi', 於 marking the man asked (as 17.6). 何如 'how, what must be so' (何如斯 as 13.20); 斯 'then'; 可以 'can'; 從政 cóng zhèng 'to take part in government' (6.6). 尊 'to honour, to hold high'. 屏 is bǐng 'to put away, to remove' — Zhu Xi gives no mark; Kong Anguo in He Yan: 屏除也. 美 'excellence, a fine thing'; 惡 è 'an evil, a bad thing'; Mr Li's remark at 17.6 names these five and four as unlike the style of the text around them. 惠 'kind, generous'; 費 fèi 'to waste, to spend' (費芳味反). 勞 láo 'to set (people) to toil' (as 19.10); 怨 'to resent'. 貪 tān 'greedy'. 泰而不驕 'assured and not haughty' is 13.26; 威而不猛 'imposing and yet not fierce' is 7.37, said there of the Master himself. Variant: He Yan's text reads 子張問政於孔子, 'asked Kongzi about government'.

sentences.t:
子張曰：「何謂惠而不費？」
子曰：「
因民之所利而利之，斯不亦惠而不費乎？
擇可勞而勞之，又誰怨？
欲仁而得仁，又焉貪？
君子無衆寡，無小大，無敢慢，斯不亦泰而不驕乎？
君子正其衣冠，尊其瞻視，儼然人望而畏之，斯不亦威而不猛乎？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zizhang said: “What is meant by kind and not wasteful?”
The Master said:
“Going by what profits the people and profiting them by it — is this not indeed kind and not wasteful?
Choosing what may be toiled at and setting them to toil at it — then who would resent it?
Desiring humaneness and getting humaneness — then how would one be greedy?
The gentleman, whether they be many or few, whether small or great, never dares slight them — is this not indeed assured and not haughty?
The gentleman sets his robes and cap straight, makes his gaze dignified; grave — people look on him and stand in awe of him — is this not indeed imposing and yet not fierce?”
sentences.i: Zizhang said: “What do you mean by generous without being lavish?” The Master said: “To give the people the benefit of what already benefits them — is that not generous without being lavish? Pick out the work that can fairly be asked of them and set them to it, and who will bear a grudge? Want humaneness and have it, and what is left to be greedy for? Whether he has many to deal with or few, great or small, the gentleman never dares treat any of them lightly — is that not quiet assurance without pride? He keeps his robes and cap in order and his gaze steady and grave, so that people look at him and are in awe — is that not commanding awe without inspiring fear?”
sentences.n: Zizhang asks only about the first of the five, and the Master answers all five. 因 'to go by, to rely on'; 民之所利 'what the people find profit in', and 利之 'to profit them (by it)'. Wang Su in He Yan: benefiting the people lies in government, with no outlay of wealth (利民在政無費於財也). 斯不亦…乎 'is this not indeed…?' (as 1.1 不亦…乎). 擇可勞 'choosing what may be toiled at'; 勞之 'to set them to toil at it'; 又 'then, moreover'. 欲仁而得仁 is said as 7.14 求仁而得仁 'sought humaneness and got humaneness'; 焉 is yān 'how' (焉於䖍反); 貪 tān 'greedy'. 無衆寡，無小大 'whether many or few, whether small or great'; 慢 'to slight, to treat with disrespect' — Kong Anguo: the gentleman does not slight people for being few or small (君子不以寡小而慢也). 正 'to set straight'; 衣冠 yī guān 'robes and cap'. 尊其瞻視 'makes his gaze dignified': 尊 is a verb here, 'to make grave'; 瞻 'to gaze', 視 'to look'. 儼然 'grave, dignified' (19.9). 望而畏之 'look at him and stand in awe of him'. Zhu Xi writes no comment on this stretch beyond his sound mark for 焉. Variant: He Yan's text reads 擇其可勞而勞之, 'choosing what of it may be toiled at'.

sentences.t:
子張曰：「何謂四惡？」
子曰：「
不教而殺謂之虐，
不戒視成謂之暴，
慢令致期謂之賊，
猶之與人也，出納之吝，謂之有司。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
(the way of) the officer in charge
to manage, to be in charge of

sentences.i: Zizhang said: “And what are the four evils?” The Master said: “Executing people who were never taught is cruelty. To demand results when no warning was given is violence. To be lax with orders and then hold people to a date is to do them harm. And when something is to go to people in any case, to be close-fisted over handing it out — that is acting like an officer in charge, not like one who governs.”
sentences.n: 教 jiào 'to teach'; 殺 shā 'to kill'. 謂之 'is called (it)'. 虐 nüè — Zhu Xi: cruel and inhumane (虐謂殘酷不仁); compare 13.30, 'using untaught people to fight is called casting them off'. 戒 'to warn beforehand' — Ma Rong in He Yan: to give no warning the day before and demand success on the spot is 'looking for results' (不宿戒而責目前成爲視成也); 暴 'violence' — Zhu Xi: sudden and hasty, with no gradual approach (暴謂卒遽無漸). 慢令 'to be slack with orders'; 致期 'to fix a deadline' (致期刻期也); 期 qī. 賊 'to injure' — Zhu Xi: slack beforehand and urgent afterwards, misleading the people and then surely punishing them, is to injure them (緩於前而急於後以誤其民而必刑之是賊害之也). 猶之 is, Zhu Xi says, like 均之 'all the same, in any case' (猶之猶言均之也); 與 yǔ 'to give'. 出 chū 'to give out' — Zhu Xi marks it 出去聲, the old reading for giving out; modern practice keeps chū. 納 nà 'to take in'; 出納 is the handing out and taking in of goods. 吝 'grudging'. 有司 'the officer in charge' (13.2): Zhu Xi: if, when things are to go to people in any case, one is grudging and irresolute at the moment of handing them out, that is the business of an officer in charge and not the substance of governing (則是有司之事而非為政之體); however much is given, people will not feel the kindness. He cites Xiang Yu 項羽, who, when men had earned a fief and the seal had been carved, could not bring himself to give it and turned it in his hand till its corners wore off, and so came to his ruin. Kong Anguo in He Yan: grudging and sparing in handing out what should be given is the task of an officer in charge, not the way of a ruler (此有司之任耳非人君之道也). Zhu Xi closes the chapter with Yin Tun: of all who asked about government, none had an answer so complete; it is recorded to follow the government of the emperors and kings, so that the Master's way of governing may be known (故記之以繼帝王之治則夫子之為政可知也). He Yan's text writes 出内, the old form of 出納.

sentences.t: 子曰：「不知命，無以為君子也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: The Master said: “Not knowing the decree, one has no means to be a gentleman.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If you do not know what is decreed, you cannot be a gentleman.”
sentences.n: 命 'decree, what Heaven ordains' (2.4 知天命, 'knew the decree of Heaven'; 16.8). 無以 'to have no means to'; 為 wéi 'to be'. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: to know the decree is to know that there is a decree and to trust it (知命者知有命而信之也); a man who does not know it will flee whenever he sees harm and rush whenever he sees profit — how can he be a gentleman? Kong Anguo in He Yan: 命 is the allotment of failure and success (命謂窮達之分也). The Master's words run on past Zhu Xi's comments into the next two units, which are left unquoted. Variant: both Ruan's text and He Yan's read 孔子曰, 'Kongzi said'.

sentences.l: Not knowing the rites, one has nothing to stand by.
sentences.i: If you do not know the rites, you have nowhere to stand.
sentences.n: Still the Master. 立 'to stand, to take one's place', as at 16.13, where he told his son 不學禮，無以立 'not learning the rites, you have nothing to stand by', and 8.8 立於禮. Zhu Xi: without knowing the rites, the ears and eyes have nothing to rest on, and the hands and feet nowhere to be placed (不知禮則耳目無所加手足無所措).

sentences.l: Not knowing words, one has no means to know men.
sentences.i: If you do not know how to weigh what people say, you cannot know what they are.
sentences.n: Still the Master. 言 'words, what people say'; 知人 'to know men'. Zhu Xi: from the rights and wrongs of a man's words one can know whether he is crooked or upright (言之得失可以知人之邪正); Ma Rong in He Yan: hearing words, one tells right from wrong (聴言則别其是非也). These are the last words of the Analects. Zhu Xi closes with Yin Tun: know these three and the gentleman's business is complete; that the disciples recorded this to end the book cannot be without purpose (弟子記此以終篇得無意乎). A learner who reads it when young and in old age does not know a single saying he can use — is he not close to making game of the sage's words (不幾於侮聖言者乎, 16.8)? He is one who offends against the Master; can he fail to take it to heart?
